title: Returning trusts
hookLine: the night he left Mecca, the Prophet left Ali behind to give back other people's things
tomorrow: if you got one sentence at the very end, which one?

cards: It's night in Mecca, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is about to leave the city for good, with men plotting against him. He is taking almost no one. But he leaves someone behind on purpose: his young cousin, Ali.

Tradition says Ali lay down in the Prophet's own bed that night. The reason he stayed is the surprising part. People of Mecca, including some who rejected his message, had left their valuables in the Prophet's keeping.
And he wasn't leaving with a single one.

teach.b: So Ali stayed, the early biographies say, and handed each deposit back to its owner before he followed. Notice the timing. The people getting their things back were the city that had just pushed the Prophet out.
He could have called it even. He didn't.
The Qur'an makes it a command, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners."
The Arabic word is amanah, a trust: anything placed in your hands that belongs to someone else. A borrowed charger. A friend's secret.
Money you owe. The tradition takes this seriously: a hadith in Sahih Muslim says even a martyr is forgiven everything except a debt. But it isn't meant to crush anyone.
A hadith in Bukhari says whoever takes people's money meaning to pay it back, Allah will help them repay.
The intention, and then the next step.

Before a long trip, you return the library books. Before the longest one, the tradition says: settle what you can. Worth remembering: on the night he fled, the Prophet made sure his enemies got their things back.

how: Muslims treat debts and things held in trust (amanah) as serious duties; before travel, illness or old age, some write down what they owe and what they hold for others, and the Prophet's leaving Ali to return the Meccans' deposits is a story often told about it.

o: keeping a friend's secret safe for many years
trusting people with your own valuables again
giving back what was placed in your hands

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: Allah helps the one who means to repay

s: the Prophet took the Meccans' deposits with him when he left
the early biographies say Ali stayed behind and returned each one to its owner.
the people who got their things back included some who rejected his message
he could have called it even. he didn't.
in Islam, owing money means you can't be forgiven
debt is taken seriously, but a hadith in Bukhari says Allah helps the one who means to repay.

games.q: a friend lent you a book, then said something cruel to you, and the friendship is over. the book is still on your shelf. what does the story point to?
o: give it back anyway; a trust doesn't depend on how they treat you.
keep it for now; she ended the friendship first.
donate it instead, so at least it does someone good.
games.why: Ali returned deposits to the city that had just pushed the Prophet out. a trust goes back to its owner.

practice: Bring to mind one thing in your hands that isn't yours: a borrowed book, a loan, a promise half-kept. If a short message would start settling it, write that message now, even if you send it later.
If not, decide the very next step and when you'll take it.

wordCard.voice: Returning trusts: giving back what was placed in your hands, from a borrowed thing to a debt, so that nothing is left owing.

orig.note: Arabic: a trust, something placed in your care; also trustworthiness.

carryVoice: The line for the road: all settled, or at least the next step taken. Good night from day seven of the journey home.
